title: What Is Knowledge?
description: The classical definition of knowledge and why it matters

concepts.title: The Traditional Analysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Philosophy has long asked: what does it mean to know something, rather than merely believe it?

The standard answer, often presented as the 'traditional' view (though historians debate how long it was really dominant), was the Justified True Belief (JTB) account, traceable to Plato's Meno and Theaetetus: you know that P if and only if (1) P is true, (2) you believe P, and (3) your belief is justified by good reasons.

Each condition rules out something: truth excludes false beliefs, however confidently held; belief excludes things you accept but don't genuinely hold; justification excludes believing true things for bad reasons.

concepts.title: The Three Conditions Up Close
concepts.contentHtml:
Consider each JTB condition with concrete examples:

Truth: If you believe the earth is flat, you lack knowledge regardless of how strongly you believe it. Knowledge requires the world to cooperate.

Belief: You might have overwhelming evidence that a loved one committed a crime, yet psychologically refuse to believe it. Without belief, you don't know it.

Justification: Suppose you believe it will rain because your knee aches. It does rain — but not because of your knee. Your true belief lacks the right kind of support to count as knowledge.

Together these three conditions seemed to many philosophers to be necessary and sufficient for knowledge.

concepts.title: Types of Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Epistemologists distinguish several types of knowledge:

Propositional knowledge (knowing-that): knowing that Paris is in France, that 7 is prime. This is the focus of JTB analysis.

Procedural knowledge (knowing-how): knowing how to ride a bike or play the piano. Gilbert Ryle argued this can't be fully reduced to propositions.

Acquaintance knowledge (knowing of): knowing Paris from having been there, or knowing someone personally. Bertrand Russell distinguished this from propositional knowledge.

Most epistemological debate centres on propositional knowledge, but the others raise their own deep puzzles — especially about what it means to know an experience.

title: Skepticism
description: Can we know anything at all? Classic skeptical challenges

concepts.title: The Dream Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
Descartes asked in the Meditations (1641): how do you know you are not dreaming right now? Dreams can feel completely vivid and coherent. If you cannot rule out dreaming, can you be certain about anything you perceive?

The argument is powerful because it exploits a gap between appearance and reality. You have access only to how things seem; how they are could diverge without your being able to detect it.

Descartes' goal was not to embrace skepticism but to find beliefs immune to it — the cogito ('I think, therefore I am') was his answer: even a deceived dreamer must be thinking.

concepts.title: The Evil Demon and the Brain in a Vat
concepts.contentHtml:
Descartes escalated the dream argument: what if an evil demon of supreme power is systematically deceiving you about everything — mathematics, logic, your own body?

Hilary Putnam modernised this as the brain-in-a-vat scenario: suppose your brain has been removed and is being fed perfect simulated experiences by a supercomputer. How would you know?

These thought experiments sharpen the skeptical challenge: our evidence for the external world is entirely experiential, and experience could in principle be faked. The anti-skeptic must explain why we are entitled to rule such scenarios out without simply assuming they don't obtain.

concepts.title: Responses to Skepticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Philosophers have responded to skepticism in several ways:

Contextualism (David Lewis, Stewart Cohen): 'know' is context-sensitive. In ordinary life we rightly say we know things; in skeptical philosophy seminars, standards are raised and we don't 'know' in that strict sense. Both can be true.

Moorean common sense (G.E. Moore): 'Here is one hand' — I know this more firmly than I could ever know the premises of a skeptical argument. Use the certainty of commonsense beliefs to reject skeptical premises.

Externalism (reliabilism): knowledge doesn't require you to be able to rule out skeptical scenarios; it requires your belief-forming processes to be reliably truth-tracking. If they are, you know — even if you can't prove the demon doesn't exist.

title: The Gettier Problem
description: A short paper that changed epistemology forever

concepts.title: Gettier's Counterexamples
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1963, Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper demolishing the JTB account.

Classic case: Smith and Jones are competing for a job. The boss tells Smith that Jones will get it. Jones has ten coins in his pocket. Smith infers: 'The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.' In fact, Smith gets the job — and Smith also happens to have ten coins in his pocket (unknown to him). Smith's belief is true, he believes it, and it is justified — yet intuitively he doesn't know it. The truth and the justification are accidentally disconnected.

concepts.title: Why Gettier Cases Work
concepts.contentHtml:
Gettier cases share a common structure: a belief is justified through a false lemma — an intermediate step that turns out to be wrong — and the belief ends up true for a completely different reason.

Smith's justification ran through the false belief that Jones would get the job. His conclusion was true, but by epistemic accident.

This reveals that JTB allows the truth and the justification to come apart: you can have excellent evidence for P, P can be true, and yet the truth of P can be entirely unconnected to your evidence. Many think knowledge should not tolerate this kind of epistemic luck.

concepts.title: Post-Gettier Responses
concepts.contentHtml:
Philosophers proposed many fourth-condition fixes:

No false lemmas (Harman): knowledge must not depend essentially on false intermediate beliefs. Blocks classic Gettier cases but misses others.

Causal theory (Alvin Goldman, early): the fact that makes P true must causally produce your belief. Handles many cases but struggles with mathematical knowledge.

Safety (Sosa, Williamson): you know P only if, in nearby possible worlds where you believe P via the same method, P is true. Accidental truths are ruled out because in nearby worlds you'd be wrong.

Knowledge-first (Williamson): stop analysing knowledge in terms of JTB; knowledge is the primitive mental state, and belief/justification are defined in terms of it.

title: Justification & Its Sources
description: Internalism, externalism, and where justification comes from

concepts.title: Internalism vs Externalism
concepts.contentHtml:
How do beliefs get justified? Two broad camps disagree:

Internalism: justification supervenes only on factors internal to the believer — what they are aware of or can access by reflection. Descartes was an internalist: justification must be traceable to clear and distinct ideas the believer can consciously inspect.

Externalism: justification can depend on factors outside the believer's awareness. Alvin Goldman's reliabilism is the best-known externalist view: a belief is justified if it was produced by a cognitive process that reliably yields true beliefs — regardless of whether you know this about your own processes.

concepts.title: Foundationalism and Coherentism
concepts.contentHtml:
Both views address the regress problem: if every belief needs justification, what justifies the justifiers? Two classic answers:

Foundationalism: there are basic beliefs — self-evident, incorrigible, or grounded directly in experience — that don't need further justification. All other beliefs are justified by inferential chains back to them. Descartes' cogito was intended as such a foundation.

Coherentism (Quine, BonJour): no belief is foundational; each belief is justified by how well it coheres with the entire web of beliefs. The web as a whole is tested against experience. Critics worry coherentism allows internally consistent but reality-detached belief systems.

concepts.title: Testimony and Social Epistemology
concepts.contentHtml:
Much of what we know we learned from others — teachers, books, experts, news. Testimony is a central source of knowledge, yet it raises puzzles.

Reductionism (Hume): testimonial knowledge must ultimately rest on personal experience and inductive inference about the reliability of testifiers. We have no independent reason to trust testimony.

Anti-reductionism (Reid, Coady): we are entitled to accept testimony as a default, subject to defeating evidence. Requiring personal verification of all testimony would render most knowledge impossible.

Social epistemology (Alvin Goldman, Miranda Fricker) extends this to ask how social structures — institutions, media, power relations — shape what communities know and what gets suppressed.

title: Contemporary Debates
description: Epistemic injustice, virtue epistemology, and the limits of knowing

concepts.title: Virtue Epistemology
concepts.contentHtml:
Virtue epistemology shifts focus from the properties of individual beliefs to the intellectual character of knowers.

Ernest Sosa distinguishes apt belief: a belief is apt if its truth is explained by the believer's intellectual virtue (reliable cognitive faculty). Linda Zagzebski grounds knowledge in intellectual virtues — stable dispositions like open-mindedness, thoroughness, and intellectual courage.

This approach reframes Gettier cases: Smith's belief about the coins reflects no intellectual virtue; the truth was not due to him. Knowledge, on this view, requires that your getting it right be a genuine achievement attributable to your own epistemic faculties.

concepts.title: Epistemic Injustice
concepts.contentHtml:
Miranda Fricker's Epistemic Injustice (2007) argues that social power shapes who gets to be a knower.

Testimonial injustice: a speaker receives less credibility than they deserve due to identity prejudice. A Black man's eyewitness testimony is discounted; a woman's report of her own pain is dismissed. The victim is wronged specifically in their capacity as a knower.

Hermeneutical injustice: a gap in collective interpretive resources disadvantages those whose experiences are not yet named. Before 'sexual harassment' existed as a concept, women lacked the vocabulary to understand and communicate their experience — a structural epistemic harm.

concepts.title: The Limits of Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Contemporary epistemology grapples with the limits and conditions of what can be known:

Closure: if you know P, and you know P entails Q, do you know Q? Closure seems obvious, yet it generates skeptical paradoxes (if I know I have hands, and having hands entails I'm not a brain-in-a-vat, I should know I'm not a brain-in-a-vat — but that seems too strong).

The Knowability Paradox (Fitch): if all truths are knowable, then all truths are known, which is absurd for finite knowers. This suggests some truths may be unknowable in principle.

Moral epistemology: can ethical claims be known? Moral realists say yes; expressivists say moral sentences aren't truth-apt at all. The debate links epistemology to metaethics.
